nameStory: The American lappet moth gets its name from the distinctive 'lappets' - fleshy, flap-like projections along the sides of its caterpillar. These skin folds help the larva blend in perfectly with tree bark when it presses flat against a trunk. The word 'lappet' comes from an old term for a loose fold of fabric, which these caterpillars definitely resemble!
description: The American lappet moth is a medium-sized brown moth with fuzzy, bear-like appearance that's active from spring through early fall across New England. Adults have a wingspan of about 1 to 2 inches and are covered in dense, soft scales that give them a woolly texture. Their caterpillars are even more distinctive - chunky, hairy larvae with prominent skin flaps that make them masters of camouflage. These moths belong to the lappet moth family, known for their particularly furry appearance.

idTips.label: Fuzzy body texture
idTips.description: The entire moth feels incredibly soft and woolly to the touch, almost like a tiny stuffed animal with dense, plush scales covering wings and body

idTips.label: Brown coloration
idTips.description: Overall brownish appearance with subtle variations in tone, often with darker and lighter bands or patches across the wings

idTips.label: Medium wingspan
idTips.description: Wings span roughly 1-2 inches across when fully extended, making them noticeably smaller than luna moths but larger than many micro-moths

idTips.label: Stocky build
idTips.description: Has a robust, compact body rather than the slender build of many other moth families, giving it a sturdy appearance

idTips.label: Caterpillar lappets
idTips.description: If you find the larva, look for distinctive fleshy flaps along the sides that feel soft and help it lie flat against bark

habitat: Look for American lappet moths in mixed deciduous forests and woodland edges throughout New England, especially areas with birches, oaks, willows, and alders. They prefer mature forests with diverse tree species rather than monoculture plantings. You'll often find them near wetland edges where willows and alders grow, as these are favorite host plants for their caterpillars.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in May in northern New England, with peak activity in late spring. Look for them at porch lights or flying around deciduous trees at dusk.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for adult moths continues through July and August. Caterpillars are actively feeding on tree leaves and may be found pressed against bark during the day.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down by early fall in northern areas, though some individuals may still be active in September. Caterpillars are preparing for winter.
seasonality.winter: Moths overwinter as pupae or late-stage caterpillars. No adult activity during the cold months - they're tucked away waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: Lappet moth caterpillars are incredible shape-shifters that can completely flatten themselves against tree bark, with their fleshy side-flaps spreading out to eliminate any telltale shadow - making them virtually invisible even when you're looking right at them!
confusionNotes: American lappet moths are most easily confused with other brown, fuzzy moths in the same family, but their particularly woolly texture and medium size help distinguish them. Remember: if it feels like petting a tiny teddy bear, you've probably found a lappet moth!
contextualKnowledge: The term 'lappet' might sound unfamiliar, but it's an old textile term that perfectly describes these caterpillars' most distinctive feature. Unlike many moth families where adults are the showstoppers, lappet moths are actually more famous for their amazing camouflaged caterpillars than their relatively plain brown adults.
compareHints: Since the American lappet moth is the only Phyllodesma species in New England, compare it to other members of the lappet moth family (Lasiocampidae). American lappets are generally smaller and more uniformly brown than tent caterpillar moths, and lack the distinctive white spots often seen on forest tent moth adults. Their texture is consistently fuzzy rather than having smooth patches like some related species.
